name: Rwanda
summary: A kingdom in the hills of East Africa, colonised by Germany and Belgium; in 1994 about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, were killed in the genocide against the Tutsi.

terrain.value: “Land of a thousand hills”: steep green hills and mountains, the Virunga volcanoes in the north-west and Lake Kivu in the west.

climate.value: A mild tropical highland climate, cooled by altitude, with two rainy seasons (about February–May and September–December).

resources.value: Fertile volcanic soils for coffee and tea, minerals such as tin, tantalum (coltan) and tungsten, and mountain gorillas for tourism.

disasters.value: Heavy rains cause landslides and floods, as in May 2023 in the north and west; droughts hit the east.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural but urbanising fast; Kigali, the capital, has more than 1 million people.

disease.value: Malaria remains common; health insurance and community health workers have greatly reduced child deaths since 2000.

migration.value: Over 2 million people fled to neighbouring countries in 1994; earlier, many Tutsi had fled in 1959–62.

economicBase.value: Services 52%, industry 22% and agriculture 20% of GDP; agriculture employs 64.5% of workers; coffee and tea are the main cash crops; tourism (over 1.4 million visitors in 2023, about US$620 million) is the leading foreign-exchange earner.

tradeRoutes.value: Goods travel by road along the Northern Corridor to Mombasa (Kenya) and the Central Corridor to Dar es Salaam (Tanzania).

moneyAndTax.value: The Rwandan franc, the national currency since 1964; taxes are collected by the Rwanda Revenue Authority.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: The infobox calls it a semi-presidential republic under an authoritarian dictatorship; the text calls it a de facto one-party state ruled by the RPF since 1994.

keyRulers.value: Rwanda’s leadership changed by a coup in 1973 and by the RPF takeover in 1994, after the genocide; the present leader is not named here.

succession.value: A coup (1973); the RPF took power after the genocide (1994).

institutions.value: A two-chamber parliament in which women hold over 60% of the lower-house seats, the highest share in the world.

stability.value: The genocide against the Tutsi (April–July 1994) killed about 800,000 people; the country has been stable since about 2000.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: The Rwanda Defence Force, formed from the former rebel army after 1994, is known for its role in UN peacekeeping missions.

majorWars.value: Genocide from 6 April 1994, lasting about 100 days: between 500,000 and 1,000,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu were killed; the RPF controlled the country by mid-July.

territoryChange.value: No change since independence in 1962, when the Belgian territory of Ruanda-Urundi was split into Rwanda and Burundi.

alliancesRivals.value: Member of the East African Community (since 2007) and the Commonwealth (since 2009); tense relations with the DR Congo.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: About three-quarters of adults can read; the University of Rwanda was formed in 2013 by merging public colleges.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Roads link Kigali to Uganda, Tanzania and Burundi; Kigali International Airport is the base of the national airline, RwandAir.

religion.value: Infobox: Christianity 93.8%, no religion 3.0%, Islam 2.2%. 2012 census: Catholic 43.7%, Protestant 37.7%, Seventh-day Adventist 11.8%, Muslim 2.0%.

languageWriting.value: Kinyarwanda is spoken by almost everyone; French, English (official since 2003) and Swahili (since 2017) are also official.

artsArchitecture.value: Imigongo art made from cow dung in geometric patterns, intore dance, and the rebuilt royal palace at Nyanza.

socialStructure.value: Ethnic labels were officially removed after 1994.

sharedIdentity.value: The state promotes a single Rwandan identity (“Ndi Umunyarwanda”, I am Rwandan) instead of ethnic labels.

dailyLife.value: Most families farm small plots and eat beans, bananas, sweet potatoes and cassava; Umuganda community work is held monthly.

neighbours.value: Uganda to the north, Tanzania to the east, Burundi to the south and the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the west.

colonisation.value: German rule from 1897 as part of German East Africa; Belgian rule from 1916 (Ruanda-Urundi, 1916–1962).

riseSignals.value: In the 15th century one kingdom under King Gihanga absorbed several neighbours; it reached its greatest extent in the 19th century under Kigeli Rwabugiri.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; rapid recovery and growth since the 2000s are often noted.

declineSignals.value: The genocide against the Tutsi (1994) killed about 800,000 people and left the country devastated.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
